# Cleaning: Missing Values, Duplicates, Outliers, Leakage {#sec-cleaning}

Cleaning is usually presented as housekeeping: fill the gaps, drop the copies, clip the
extremes, then get on with modeling. Each of those steps pulls a lever, though. Dropping rows
changes the sampling distribution $q$; filling a gap changes the representation; and the way a
step is fit can change what an evaluation measures. This chapter derives what three common
treatments of missing values do under each kind of missingness, then measures two leaks of very
different size.

## The problem

A dataset arrives with some values missing, some rows repeated, some values extreme, and a
plan to fit preprocessing steps before the model. For each treatment, which quantities stay
correct, and which become biased? The answer depends less on the treatment than on *why* the
data looks the way it does.

## Assumptions

1. **Missingness has a mechanism.** Following Rubin (1976), van Buuren states the three cases
   this way: data are **MCAR** "if the probability of being missing is the same for all
   cases", **MAR** "if the probability of being missing is the same only within groups
   defined by the observed data", and **MNAR** if neither holds [@vanbuuren2018fimd, §1.2].
   Which case applies cannot be read off the observed data alone: it is an assumption about
   $p$.
2. **One column goes missing, and a correlated column is always observed.** With several
   incomplete columns the reasoning is the same, but the bookkeeping is not.
3. **Test examples will be new.** Deployment does not show the model copies of its training
   rows. If it does (a lookup service, repeat customers), duplicates are part of $p$, and
   removing them would be wrong.

## Derivation or demonstration

**Missing values.** Consider column $z_1$ of the tabular testbed, with true mean 0 and variance
1, 40% missing, and an always-observed column $z_2$ correlated 0.6 with it. Three treatments:

- **Complete-case analysis** drops the rows where $z_1$ is missing. It changes $q$: the kept
  rows are a selection, and [The Data-Generating Process](01-the-data-generating-process.qmd#sec-dgp)
  showed what selection does.
- **Mean imputation** fills each gap with the observed mean. It changes the representation:
  a missing value is now encoded as an ordinary-looking number.
- **Regression imputation** fills each gap with the straight-line prediction from $z_2$, fit
  on the rows where $z_1$ is observed.

Under MCAR the kept rows are a random subset, so complete-case estimates are unbiased. Mean
imputation keeps the mean but puts 40% of the values exactly at it. Its variance falls to about $1 - r$
times the original, $0.6$ here, with $r$ the share imputed. Regression imputation keeps the part of
the variance that $z_2$ explains: imputed values have variance $0.6^2$ of the original, so the
total is $1 - 0.4\,(1 - 0.6^2) = 0.744$. Over 200 seeds the measured variances were 0.995,
0.596 and 0.740.

Under MAR, here a missingness probability that rises with $z_2$, the observed $z_1$ values are
skewed toward one side. Both the complete-case mean and the mean-imputed mean were $-0.321$ on
average. Regression imputation uses exactly the variable that drives the missingness, and its
mean was $-0.002$. Under MNAR, missingness rising with $z_1$ itself, every treatment was biased.
The best of the three was regression imputation, at $-0.392$
(`tests/test_missing.py::test_mcar_mean_imputation_shrinks_variance_mar_complete_case_biased`).

::: {.callout-note title="Result: the mechanism decides which treatment is biased"}
A complete-case estimate of the mean is unbiased under MCAR, and biased here under MAR and MNAR.
(Regressions fit to complete cases can stay unbiased when missingness depends only on the
regression's inputs: that is selection on $x$, from
[The Data-Generating Process](01-the-data-generating-process.qmd#sec-dgp).) Mean imputation
keeps the mean under MCAR only, and always shrinks the variance, by the share imputed. Regression imputation on the
variables that drive the missingness removes the bias of the mean under MAR, but understates
the variance. No treatment that uses only the observed data removes the bias under MNAR.
:::

These match van Buuren's summary of the same methods. Listwise deletion gives "unbiased
estimates of means, variances and regression weights" under MCAR. Mean imputation will
"underestimate the variance". And under regression imputation "correlations are biased
upwards, and the variability of the imputed data is systematically underestimated"
[@vanbuuren2018fimd, §1.3]. Multiple imputation, which adds the missing variability back by
drawing several plausible values, is the standard remedy; it is beyond this book and
@vanbuuren2018fimd treats it in full.

**Duplicates.** If some test rows are copies of training rows, a model that memorizes is
rewarded twice. On T1, a 1-nearest-neighbor classifier trained on 2,000 rows scored 0.660 on
1,000 fresh test rows. With 30% of the test rows replaced by training rows, it scored 0.762,
and with half, 0.830. The Bayes accuracy, the most any classifier can reach on new data, is
0.749. A test score above it is impossible on new data, so it measures memorization. On the
fresh rows alone, the score stayed at 0.660 (20 seeds;
`tests/test_leakage.py::test_train_test_duplicates_inflate_the_test_score`).

{{< include ../includes/cards/dedup-train-test.md >}}

**Leakage through fitted preprocessing.** Kaufman et al. define leakage as "the introduction
of information about the data mining target, which should not be legitimately available to
mine from". They separate leaking features from leakage in training examples
[@kaufman2011leakage, §3.2–3.3]. scikit-learn's documentation gives the practical rule: never
call `fit` on the test data. It says the risk applies to "almost all transformations in
scikit-learn, including (but not limited to) `StandardScaler`, `SimpleImputer`, and `PCA`"
(scikit-learn 1.9, *Common pitfalls*, §12.2).

The rule is right. The sizes of the two leaks it guards against are very different, though.
On i.i.d. T1 data, a scaler, a min-max scaler or a mean imputer fit on train plus test instead
of train alone changed test accuracy by at most 0.4 percentage points on average. That held for
a 15-nearest-neighbor classifier and a strongly regularized logistic regression, over 200 seeds
each. The changes were not consistently upward: the largest was $-0.4$ points. These steps see
the test *inputs*, whose distribution matches the training inputs, and never the test labels.

A supervised step is different. With 100 examples, 2,000 pure-noise features and labels that
are coin flips, selecting the 20 features most associated with the labels on all the data,
then cross-validating a classifier on them, reported an accuracy of 0.825. The same selection
done inside each fold reported 0.513, close to the true 0.5 (20 seeds;
`tests/test_leakage.py::test_fitting_preprocessing_on_test_is_optimistic`).

::: {.callout-note title="Result: what a leak leaks"}
Fitting a step on the test data leaks what that step reads. An unsupervised step reads the
test inputs, which on i.i.d. data carry little that the training inputs do not. A supervised
step reads the test labels, and can fabricate a signal from noise.
:::

{{< include ../includes/cards/train-only-fitting.md >}}

::: {.callout-note title="In practice"}
Put every fitted step in a `sklearn.pipeline.Pipeline` and cross-validate the pipeline as one
estimator, so each step is refit inside each fold. scikit-learn 1.9's `SimpleImputer` imputes the mean by
default (`strategy="mean"`); `add_indicator=True` also appends a column marking which values
were missing, which keeps the fact of missingness available to the model. That fact is itself
informative whenever the data is not MCAR.
:::

**Outliers.** An extreme value is either an error (a unit mix-up, a sensor fault) or a real
case from the tail of $p$. The two call for opposite treatments. Removing errors corrects the
representation. Removing real tail cases changes $q$ and teaches the model that the tail does
not exist. No statistic separates them reliably, because both are, by definition, rare.
[Affine Scaling](05-affine-scaling.qmd#sec-affine) shows how one scaler is built to be
insensitive to them, and robust losses are derived in
[loss-functions-lab](https://ioannisantoniadis.github.io/loss-functions-lab/chapters/05-laplace-robust-losses.html).

## What it does to the learned model

Missing-value treatments change the data a model is fit to in ways the model cannot detect. A
mean-imputed column is a mixture of real values and a spike at the mean. A linear model fits a
slope through both. A tree can split the spike off and use "was missing" as information, which
under MAR or MNAR is real information. Complete-case analysis under MAR is selection: the model
is fit to a distribution that differs from $p$.

Duplicates and leaks change nothing about the model itself, only what we believe of it. Their
cost appears later, when the deployed model performs as the fresh rows predicted, not as the
contaminated test set promised.

## Failure modes

![Estimated mean (A) and variance (B) of $z_1$ after complete-case analysis, mean imputation and regression imputation, under MCAR, MAR and MNAR missingness (40% missing; dots are 200 seeds, bars their means). Which treatment is biased depends on the mechanism: mean imputation keeps the MCAR mean but shrinks the variance, regression imputation repairs the MAR mean, and nothing here repairs MNAR.](../images/missingness.png){#fig-missingness}

![Panel A: 1-nearest-neighbor test accuracy as a growing share of the test rows are copies of training rows, on the contaminated test set and on its fresh rows only (mean and range over 20 seeds); above the Bayes accuracy is impossible on new data. Panel B: the change in test accuracy from fitting a preprocessing step on train plus test instead of train alone, for unsupervised steps (200 seeds each) and for supervised feature selection on pure-noise labels (20 seeds). Duplicates and supervised steps inflate the score; unsupervised steps barely move it.](../images/leakage.png){#fig-leakage}

@fig-missingness and @fig-leakage show the failures measured above. Three more:

- **Assuming MAR when the data is MNAR.** Income goes unreported more often when it is high;
  a symptom goes unrecorded when it is absent. No observed column carries that dependence, so
  imputation from observed columns cannot remove it.
- **Near-duplicates.** Exact matching finds copied rows, not a resized image or a reformatted
  record. [Choosing Data](14-choosing-data.qmd#sec-choosing-data) returns to deduplication at
  scale.
- **Supervised steps hidden in "preprocessing".** Target encoding, feature selection by
  correlation, and resampling to balance classes all read the labels. Fit before the split,
  each is a leak of the second kind. Target encoding is the subject of
  [Encoding and Features](07-encoding-and-features.qmd#sec-encoding).

## What the toy cannot show

The testbed's missingness depends on one column through a known curve, and its duplicates are
exact. Real missingness mixes mechanisms, and which one holds cannot be tested from the
observed data. The demonstrations show what each treatment does under each mechanism, not
which mechanism a real dataset has.
